summary: **Parties Present:** Shri Shailesh Verma, Advocate, SPPL Ms. Chandani Bhatia, Advocate, SPPL Shri D. D. Chopra, Sr. Advocate, SPPL Shri Sanyam Agarwal, Advocate, SPPL Shri Gajendra Sinh Vasava, NLDC Shri Ashok Ranjan, NLDC Ms. Himani Dutta, NLDC Shri Alok Mishra, NLDC Ms. Anisha Chopra, NLDC - (iii) issue any other order or direction as this Learned Commission may deem fit and proper in the facts and circumstances of the case. - (g) The Petitioner’s co-generation plants have been erroneously treated as captive generating stations by the NLDC, and consequently, the Petitioner has been wrongfully denied permission to trade in the RECs issued against its self-consumption 6. The counsel for the Petitioner, vide its letter dated 12.8.2025, sought an adjournment due to the non-availability of the arguing counsel. Considering the said request, the Commission adjourned the matter. Respondent further sought liberty to file a comprehensive reply addressing both the maintainability and the merits of the present Petition. Considering the submissions, the Commission permitted the Respondent, NLDC, to file its comprehensive reply, on maintainability as well as merits, within four weeks. The Commission also granted the Petitioner three weeks thereafter to file its rejoinder, if any - (c) The regulatory distinction applied to the Petitioner is justified by paragraph 4.83 of the Statement of Reasons to the REC Regulations 2022. The provisions specified in the regulation adequately explain the clear distinction between "self-consumption" and "captive consumption". The prior distinction created by this Commission under the proviso to Regulation 5(1)(b) of the REC Regulations 2010, which previously allowed issuing RECs to cogeneration plants to the extent of their captive consumption, has been purposely excluded from the new REC Regulations 2022, thereby substantiating the denial of tradeable RECs to the Petitioner under the current framework. 9. During the subsequent hearing on 3.12.2025, the learned counsel for the Petitioner, SPPL, requested additional time to file its rejoinder. Allowing this request, the Commission permitted the Petitioner to file its rejoinder within two weeks and directed that the Petition be listed for the next hearing on 12.2.2026. # ** Rejoinder by the Petitioner, SPPL, dated 13.12.2025, on the Reply submitted by the NLDC ** 10. The Petitioner, SPPL, in its rejoinder dated 13.12.2025, disputed the averments made by the Respondent, NLDC, and submitted the following: - (d) Further, the continuous issuance of non-tradeable RECs to the Petitioner was alleged to be in direct contravention of the REC Regulations, 2022, as the Respondents had wrongly implemented the framework by treating the Petitioner as a captive generating station instead of a renewable energy generating station eligible for tradeable RECs. Consequently, the Petitioner maintained that its grievances squarely fell within the ambit of Regulation 17 of the REC Regulations, 2022, which expressly authorises the Commission to pass orders and issue directions to resolve implementation issues. 11. During the course of the proceedings, the learned senior counsel for the Petitioner and the representative of the Respondent, NLDC, advanced and formally concluded their respective arguments pertaining to the Petitioner's prayer for regulatory compliance under Regulation 17 of the REC Regulations, 2022. After both parties concluded their submissions, the Commission reserved the matter for its final order. 12. The Commission has heard the learned counsels for the Petitioner and the Respondent and has carefully perused the records. Briefly, the Petitioner, SPPL, is a co-generation power company operating two facilities at village Chilwaria, District Bahraich, U.P. (32 MW and 18 MW units), and at village Simbhaoli, District Hapur, U.P. (34 MW and 28 MW units), integrated with sugar manufacturing operations. The Petitioner's two projects have been registered under the REC mechanism since 25.10.2016. Under the CERC REC Regulations, 2010 and its amendments, the Central Agency issued tradable Renewable Energy Certificates to these projects until November 2022. The REC Regulations, 2022 came into force on 05.12.2022, repealing the prior REC Regulations, 2010. Post 05.12.2022, the Respondent, NLDC, acting as the Central Agency, began issuing RECs to the Petitioner against selfconsumption of electricity at both co-generation facilities as non-tradable certificates. The Petitioner has filed the present petition seeking directions to allow trading of these RECs, contending that its co-generation plants do not qualify as captive generating stations and that 17. The Commission has also considered Paragraph 4.83 of the Statement of Reasons (SoR) to the REC Regulations, 2022, relied upon by the NLDC. The relevant extract of Paragraph 4.83 reads as follows: - (c) The prayers made by the Petitioner, Simbhaoli Power Private Limited, in the present petition are not sustainable and are accordingly dismissed.
title: Seeking regulatory compliance by issuing a direction for the National Load Dispatch Centre, the Central Agency, under Regulation-17 of the CERC (Terms and Conditions for Renewable Energy Certificate Regulations-2022) for allowing the Petitioner to trade Renewable Energy Certificates issued to the Petitioner against self-consumption of electricity at its co-generation facilities located at vill. Chilwaria, district Bahraich, UP and vill. Simbhaoli, district Hapur, UP Simbhaoli Power Private Ltd
